title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])
word: Teach us to number our days
hookLine: a thousand years are as yesterday to God

cards: Time is strange. A bad afternoon at the dentist lasts forever. A whole summer vanishes.
A photo from ten years ago feels like last month. Next week's calendar is already full. Then comes the moment of looking up and asking: where did it all go?
The oldest voice in the whole psalter, by tradition, asked the same thing, and asked God to teach him what to do about it.

teach.b: Psalm 89 in the Douay, 90 in most Bibles, carries the heading a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It starts with God's time: "Lord, thou hast been our refuge from generation to generation."

Before the mountains were born, before the earth was formed, from eternity to eternity, you are God. Then our time: "For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which is past. And as a watch in the night."
A watch was a shift of guard duty, a few hours.

teach.h: A THOUSAND YEARS, ONE NIGHT SHIFT.
teach.b: A thousand years, to God, is one night shift. The New Testament echoes it: "one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And human life?
Like grass: in the morning it springs up and flowers; by evening it's cut down and dry. Our years are seventy, the psalm says, or eighty if we're strong, and they're gone quickly, and we fly away.

Then the line in today's title, the way the Hebrew and the King James have it: teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. Counting the days isn't morbid here. It's the road to a wise heart.

A surprise for Douay readers: the old Latin, and the Douay after it, read that verse quite differently, as a prayer that God make his right hand known, and hearts be taught in wisdom. Same hope, different road.
The psalm ends asking God to satisfy us in the morning with mercy, and to establish the work of our hands.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 89 [90] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, when the readings turn to the shortness of life.

games.q: what does “teach us to number our days” mean?
o: count your short life so you grow wise
keep a careful diary of every day
work out the exact date the world ends

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: as yesterday, or one night watch
grass, green at morning, dry by evening
the road to a heart of wisdom

s: the Douay-Rheims reads teach us to number our days
the Latin and the Douay read that verse differently: a prayer that God make his right hand known, and hearts be taught in wisdom.
the psalm's heading calls it a prayer of Moses
a prayer of Moses the man of God.
the psalm says counting your days is morbid
it's how you get a heart of wisdom.

games.q: the psalm has just said life is like grass that withers by evening. what does it ask God for next?
o: to be taught to number our days, for a heart of wisdom.
games.why: not more time, but wisdom about the time there is: teach us to number our days.

practice: Look at the time and work out roughly how many waking hours you have left today: four, nine?
Hold that number with attention, not panic, and ask what one thing you'd most want those hours to hold: a conversation, a task, rest, kindness.
If you pray, ask as the psalm does, teach me to number my days; if you don't, let the number sharpen what matters.

wordCard.voice: Teach us to number our days. The prayer of Moses: our time is short, so let counting it make us wise. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: number your days. Grass by evening, wisdom by morning. Day one hundred seventy-four, counted.
